summary: Fluent addition and subtraction within 100 means computing accurately AND choosing an efficient strategy for the particular numbers, not running one algorithm for everything. Learners partition into tens and ones, compensate near a ten, use known facts, count up to find a difference between close numbers, and exploit the inverse to check. The target is flexible, justified computation, built on secure single-digit recall. The core activity places the same calculation on two tools so the learner feels why the smart method depends on the numbers; supporting activities add strategy-selection practice, a worked strategy reference, and spoken justification.
misconceptions: Smaller-from-larger subtraction bug: in 83−25 doing 5−3 in the ones column, answer 62
Partitioning correctly but dropping or mis-recombining the regrouped ten (46+37 → 73)
Applying one written method rigidly even when the numbers make a mental strategy far quicker (column-subtracting 71−68)
Treating addition and subtraction as unrelated, so the inverse is not used to check

activities.title: Same calculation, two tools: feel which method fits the numbers
steps: Take 71 − 68 and first work it on a base-ten column workspace: there are not enough ones, so decompose a ten, cross out, and carry through the several steps of the borrow.
Now work the same 71 − 68 on a number line: count up from 68 to 71 and see the difference is just three.
Place the three-hop count-up beside the multi-step borrow and say which was quicker and why.
Switch to 46 + 37 on the base-ten side: combine 40+30 and 6+7, compose the thirteen ones into one ten and three, and add that ten in so the total is 83, not 73.
Finish by looking at a fresh pair of numbers and stating, before you start, which method you will use and why.
activities.insight: The efficient method depends on the numbers: when the numbers are close, counting up the difference beats a columnar borrow; regrouping must be composed or decomposed deliberately so the extra ten is never silently dropped.

activities.title: Check with the inverse and solve missing-number problems
steps: After computing 83 − 25, add your answer back to 25 and confirm it returns to 83.
Given a missing-number problem such as 46 + ? = 83, use subtraction (83 − 46) to find the unknown, then add back to check.
State in words how addition and subtraction undo each other for the pair you just solved.
activities.insight: Addition and subtraction are inverse operations, so adding an answer back is a reliable self-check and lets you turn a missing-number problem into the operation you find easier.

activities.title: Match the calculation to the smartest strategy (selection practice)
steps: Across a mixed set of additions and subtractions, pair each calculation with the most efficient strategy (partition, compensate near a ten, count up the difference, or recall a known fact).
For 83 − 25, choose the correct answer (58) and explain why 62 is wrong.
Say aloud what feature of the numbers made you pick that strategy.
activities.insight: Reading the numbers first—how close they are, whether they sit near a ten, whether a fact is known—tells you which method is efficient before you compute.

activities.title: Worked strategy reference to consult
steps: Reveal, for each calculation type, its most efficient method and a short reason: partitioning for 46 + 37, counting up for 71 − 68, compensation for numbers near a ten.
Compare a worked example with your own jotting on a similar pair to see whether your recombination kept the regrouped ten.
activities.insight: Each strategy has a signature of numbers it suits; a worked example makes the method and its justification explicit.

activities.title: Justify your method aloud
steps: After solving a pair, explain to a partner or adult why you chose your method for those particular numbers.
Respond to a prompt such as: 'You borrowed for 71 − 68—can you see a quicker way to find the gap between 68 and 71?' and try the alternative.
activities.insight: Being able to justify a strategy choice out loud consolidates the habit of reading the numbers before computing.

checkQuestion: Set these four one at a time and watch the child work each, letting them choose their own method and jot: 46 + 37, then 83 − 25, then 60 − 24, then 71 − 68. Pay particular attention to which method they reach for on 71 − 68.
checkAnswer: 83, 58, 36, 3. Fluent work: 46+37 by partitioning (70+13=83); 83−25 by regrouping or counting up; 60−24 as 60−20−4 or by counting up from 24; 71−68 should trigger counting up (68→71 = 3) rather than columnar borrowing.
